claims.text: Adding 2–3 at% Co to MnNiSi-based alloys will promote fine, coherent Co-rich precipitates.
The Co-rich precipitates will refine the microstructure.
Fine Co-rich precipitates will act as crack-arresting features.
The Co addition and resulting microstructure will significantly improve mechanical performance.
The Co-doped alloy will retain a large magnetocaloric response.
Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization and annealing at 800–850 °C for 30–60 seconds will produce a uniform nanoscale distribution of Co-rich precipitates.
Systematic magnetic characterization during processing can ensure that precipitate size and distribution do not adversely shift the magnetostructural transition.
The Co-rich precipitates will occur both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Co has a modest atomic-size mismatch relative to the base elements that induces localized lattice distortions.
The localized lattice distortions caused by Co favor nucleation of fine Co-rich precipitates.
The precipitates reinforce grain boundaries and resist crack propagation.
The precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitate-mediated crack arrest and barriers to dislocation motion will enhance ductility and fracture toughness.
Coherency of the precipitates will minimize interference with the magnetostructural transition.
Relative to an identically processed undoped alloy, the Co-doped alloy will have increased fracture toughness and ductility.
Co doping will not significantly change magnetic entropy change or transition temperature relative to the undoped alloy.
Mechanical improvement while retaining magnetocaloric performance will occur only when processing yields uniformly dispersed, fine Co-rich precipitates.
Excessive Co addition or unsuitable heat treatment could produce coarser precipitates.
Excessive Co addition or unsuitable heat treatment could shift the magnetostructural transition and compromise the magnetocaloric effect.
